column2: [OSI] The 7 OSI layers, bottom (1) to top (7)
column3: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application   (Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away)
Physical: bits as electrical/light/radio signals — cables, connectors, signaling, hubs, repeaters
Data Link: frames between devices on the SAME local network, using MAC addresses — switches, bridges, NICs, Ethernet, 802.11
Network: packets between DIFFERENT networks using logical (IP) addresses and routing — routers, L3 switches, IP, ICMP, IPsec
Transport: end-to-end delivery between applications using port numbers — TCP (reliable) and UDP (best effort)
Session: sets up, maintains and tears down sessions between applications (dialog control)
Presentation: formats/translates data — encoding, compression, encryption (e.g. TLS/SSL is often placed here, JPEG, ASCII)
Application: network services applications use — HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP, SSH (the protocol, not the app itself)
LLC (Logical Link Control, talks to layer 3) and MAC (Media Access Control, addressing + media access)

Device airflow direction — must match the rack's hot aisle/cold aisle layout or the gear recirculates hot air
Racks face alternate directions so intakes share a cold aisle and exhausts share a hot aisle
Termination point where permanent cable runs land, so you patch to switches with short cords
Same idea for fiber — terminates and organizes fiber runs
Physical security for equipment in shared spaces
Uninterruptible Power Supply — battery that covers short outages, smooths dips/surges, gives time to shut down or start a generator
Power Distribution Unit — rack power strip that feeds the gear; metered/managed PDUs report load and allow remote outlet control
Total draw (watts/amps) of the equipment — must stay under circuit, PDU and UPS capacity
Equipment and PDUs must match the supplied voltage (e.g. 120 V vs 208/230 V)
Keep moderate (~40–60% RH): too low → static discharge (ESD); too high → condensation/corrosion
About 18–27 °C (64–81 °F) per ASHRAE
Clean-agent/gas systems (e.g. FM-200, inert gas) don't damage electronics; pre-action sprinklers keep pipes dry until a fire is detected
Long-term backup power — UPS bridges the gap until it starts
Physical: actual devices, cables, ports, locations. Logical: how traffic flows — subnets, VLANs, routing

column2: [Processes] Layer 1 network diagram — what it shows
column3: Physical cabling and connections

column2: [Processes] Layer 2 network diagram — what it shows
column3: Switches, VLANs and trunks

column2: [Processes] Layer 3 network diagram — what it shows
column3: IP subnets, routers and routing
Shows what equipment sits in which U of each rack
Documents where each cable runs and its labels, patch panel ports and endpoints
Hardware, software, licensing, warranty/support status
IP Address Management — tracks/plans IP space, subnets, DHCP scopes and DNS records in one place
Service Level Agreement — contract defining expected service (uptime %, response times) and penalties
Measures signal strength and interference across a site to plan or validate AP placement
EOL: vendor stops selling/making the product. EOS: vendor stops patches/support — a security risk

column2: [Processes] Software management: what to keep patched
column3: OS, firmware, applications — patches and bug fixes, tested and scheduled
Retiring equipment safely: sanitize/wipe configs and data, update inventory and documentation, remove from monitoring/DNS
Formal process: request → impact/risk review → approval (change board) → scheduled window with rollback plan → documentation

column2: [Processes] Change management: process tracking / service request
column3: Every change has a ticket recording what, why, who approved, and outcome
Production: the running config. Backup: saved copies for restore after failure or bad change
The approved standard config that new and existing devices are compared against
Protocol for monitoring/managing devices: a manager polls agents (UDP 161); agents send traps (UDP 162)
Unsolicited alert an agent sends to the manager when an event happens (e.g. interface down)
The database/definition of what can be monitored on a device
The identifier for one specific value in the MIB
Shared password-like string in v1/v2c, sent in cleartext. Change the defaults 'public'/'private'
v2c: community strings, no encryption. v3: per-user authentication AND encryption (authPriv) — use v3
Metadata about conversations — who talked to whom, ports, how much, when — without payloads
Records full packets (headers + payload) for deep analysis — Wireshark, tcpdump

column2: [Monitoring] Flow data vs packet capture — which for 'top talkers' over a month?
column3: Flow data (lightweight summaries). Packet capture is for deep inspection of a specific problem
What 'normal' looks like (utilization, latency, errors) — needed to detect anomalies
Alerts when metrics deviate from the baseline or thresholds
Central server that receives logs from many devices so you can search and retain them
Security Information and Event Management — collects and correlates logs across systems, alerts on security events
0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug (lower = more severe)
Tools pull/push data programmatically (REST APIs) to automate monitoring and connect systems
Switch copies traffic from ports/VLANs to a monitoring port for an IDS or analyzer
TAP: hardware inline device that copies ALL traffic, including errors, without loading the switch. SPAN: software copy on the switch, can drop under load

column2: [Monitoring] Network discovery: ad hoc vs scheduled
column3: Ad hoc: run on demand. Scheduled: periodic scans to keep inventory and maps current
Studying traffic patterns/volumes (flows, captures) to find top talkers, unusual traffic, capacity needs
Tracks latency, throughput, utilization, errors against baselines
Checks whether devices/services are up (ping, SNMP, HTTP checks) and alerts on outages
Detects config changes/drift from the baseline and alerts
Recovery Point Objective — maximum acceptable DATA loss, measured in time (backups every 4 h → RPO 4 h)
Recovery Time Objective — maximum acceptable DOWNTIME before service is restored
Mean Time To Repair — average time to fix a failure (lower is better)
Mean Time Between Failures — average uptime between failures (higher is better)
Space, power, connectivity only — no ready equipment or data; cheapest, slowest (days–weeks)
Some equipment and connectivity in place, data restored from backups; hours–days
Fully equipped, data replicated, ready almost immediately; most expensive
All nodes/sites handle traffic at the same time; failure just reduces capacity
Standby node/site idles until the active one fails, then takes over
Team talks through a disaster scenario on paper — tests the plan and roles without touching systems
Actually performs failover/restore to prove the DR plan works
Discover (client broadcast) → Offer (server) → Request (client) → Acknowledge (server)
The range of addresses a DHCP server hands out for a subnet, plus its settings
Always gives the same IP to a specific client, matched by MAC address
Addresses inside the scope that the server will never hand out (e.g. used by static devices)
How long a client may use its address; renews at 50% (T1) with its server, rebinds to any server at 87.5% (T2)
3 = default gateway (router), 6 = DNS servers, 15 = domain name, 66/67 = TFTP server/boot file (PXE)
Router forwards DHCP broadcasts from a subnet to a DHCP server on another subnet

column2: [Services] Clients on one VLAN get APIPA, other VLANs are fine — first thing to check
column3: The DHCP relay/IP helper on that VLAN's gateway (or scope exhaustion for that subnet)
IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration — host builds its own address from the router advertisement prefix + its own interface ID; no DHCP server needed
Stateful: server assigns addresses (like DHCPv4). Stateless: address via SLAAC, DHCPv6 only provides options like DNS
Hostname → IPv4 address
Hostname → IPv6 address
Alias → another hostname (www.example.com → example.com)
The mail server(s) for a domain, with priority (lower = preferred)
Arbitrary text — used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC and domain ownership verification
The authoritative name servers for a zone
IP address → hostname (reverse lookup)
Start of Authority — zone's primary server, admin contact, serial number and timers
Location (host + port) of a service, e.g. SIP, LDAP, Kerberos
Forward: name → IP. Reverse: IP → name (in-addr.arpa for IPv4, ip6.arpa for IPv6)
Authoritative: from a server that hosts the zone. Non-authoritative: from a resolver's cache
Primary holds the editable zone; secondary keeps a read-only copy via zone transfer (TCP 53) for redundancy
Recursive: 'give me the final answer' (client → resolver). Iterative: 'tell me who to ask next' (resolver → root → TLD → authoritative)
Digitally signs DNS records so resolvers can verify they're authentic and unmodified — integrity, NOT confidentiality
Both encrypt DNS queries. DoH = DNS over HTTPS (443, blends with web traffic). DoT = DNS over TLS (853)
Local name → IP table checked before DNS — /etc/hosts or C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts
Network Time Protocol (UDP 123) — syncs clocks; stratum 0 = reference clock, stratum 1 = server attached to it, and so on
Log correlation, Kerberos authentication, certificate validity, scheduled tasks
Precision Time Protocol (IEEE 1588) — sub-microsecond accuracy using hardware timestamps; finance, industrial, telecom/5G
Network Time Security — adds cryptographic authentication to NTP so time sources can't be spoofed
Permanent tunnel between two networks' gateways (routers/firewalls); users don't run a client
An individual device connects to the corporate network through a VPN client
Remote access through a web browser over TLS (SSL VPN portal) — no installed client
Split: only corporate traffic goes through the VPN, internet goes direct. Full: ALL traffic goes through the VPN (more control/inspection, more load)
SSH (CLI over network), GUI (web/HTTPS), API (automation), console (direct serial)
Direct serial/USB connection to a device's console port — works even if the network config is broken
A hardened server admins connect to first, then reach management interfaces from it — one controlled, logged entry point
In-band: manage over the production network. Out-of-band: separate path (console server, management network, cellular modem) that still works when production is down
Confidentiality (only authorized can read), Integrity (data unaltered), Availability (accessible when needed)
A weakness that could be exploited
Something or someone that could exploit a vulnerability
The method or code that actually takes advantage of a vulnerability
The likelihood × impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability

column2: [Security concepts] Encryption in transit vs at rest
column3: In transit: protects data moving over the network (TLS, IPsec). At rest: protects stored data (disk/database encryption)
Public Key Infrastructure — CAs issue certificates binding a public key to an identity so others can trust it
Signed by its own key, not a trusted CA — encrypts fine but browsers/clients warn because identity can't be verified
Authentication (who are you), Authorization (what can you do), Accounting (what did you do)
Something you know (password), have (token/phone), are (biometric) — plus somewhere you are. MFA = two+ DIFFERENT categories

column2: [Security concepts] Is a password plus a security question MFA?
column3: No — both are 'something you know'
Single Sign-On — authenticate once, access many systems
AAA protocol for network access (Wi-Fi 802.1X, VPN); UDP 1812/1813; combines authentication and authorization; encrypts only the password
Cisco AAA protocol for device administration; TCP 49; encrypts the entire payload; separates authentication, authorization and accounting (per-command authorization)

column2: [Security concepts] RADIUS vs TACACS+ — which for controlling admin commands on routers?
column3: TACACS+
Protocol to query/modify directory services (users, groups) — 389, LDAPS 636 (e.g. Active Directory)
XML-based federation standard — an identity provider vouches for the user to a service provider for web SSO
Time-based one-time passwords (TOTP — codes that change every ~30 s) and/or allowing logins only during set hours
Give users and systems only the access they need for their job, nothing more

column2: [Security concepts] Role-based vs rule-based access control
column3: Role-based: permissions by job role/group. Rule-based: permissions by rules/conditions (ACLs, time of day) applied to everyone
Allowing/denying access or actions based on a device's physical location

column2: [Security concepts] Physical security: cameras and locks
column3: Cameras deter and record; locks (key, badge, biometric) control entry
A decoy system that lures attackers so you can detect and study them
A network of honeypots
Laws requiring certain data to be stored/processed within a specific country or region
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — required security controls for anyone handling credit card data
EU regulation protecting personal data of people in the EU — consent, breach notification, right to erasure

column2: [Security concepts] Why segment IoT/IIoT, SCADA/ICS/OT, guest and BYOD devices?
column3: They're hard to patch or untrusted — isolate them on their own VLANs/zones so a compromise can't spread to critical systems
Systems that control physical industrial processes (power, water, manufacturing) — availability-critical, often legacy
Bring Your Own Device — personal devices on the network; control with NAC, MDM and a separate segment
DoS: one source overwhelms a target. DDoS: many sources (botnet) at once — much harder to block
Attacker spoofs the victim's IP and sends small requests to servers (DNS, NTP) that send large replies to the victim
Getting traffic into a VLAN you shouldn't reach — via switch spoofing or double tagging
Attacker's device negotiates a trunk (DTP) with the switch and gets all VLANs. Prevent: disable auto-trunking, hard-set access ports
Attacker on the native VLAN sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags; the first switch strips one and forwards into the target VLAN. Prevent: change native VLAN off the user VLAN/1
Flooding a switch with fake source MACs to fill its MAC table, so it floods all frames like a hub → attacker can sniff. Prevent: port security
Sending fake ARP replies so victims map the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC → on-path attack. Prevent: Dynamic ARP Inspection
Poisoning: corrupting a resolver's CACHE with false records. Spoofing: forging DNS responses to a victim. Both redirect users to malicious IPs. DNSSEC helps
Unauthorized DHCP server handing out a malicious gateway/DNS (on-path) or bad addresses. Prevent: DHCP snooping
An unauthorized AP plugged into the network (often by an employee) — a backdoor around security
Attacker's AP copying a legitimate SSID to trick users into connecting and capture traffic/credentials
Attacker secretly relays/intercepts traffic between two parties (formerly 'man-in-the-middle')
Fraudulent messages that steal credentials or deliver malware
Phishing aimed at a specific person or group
Phishing aimed at executives
Phishing by voice / phone call
Phishing by SMS text message
Searching trash for sensitive info — prevent with shredding
Watching someone's screen/keyboard to steal info — privacy screens, awareness
Following an authorized person through a secured door without badging (piggybacking = with their consent). Prevent: mantraps/access control vestibules, guards
Attaches to a host file or program and needs a user action to spread
Spreads across networks by itself — no user action needed
Disguised as legitimate software
Encrypts your data and demands payment to unlock it
Many compromised hosts remote-controlled by an attacker, often used for DDoS
Disable unused ports and services, change default passwords, update firmware, use SSH/HTTPS/SNMPv3 instead of cleartext protocols

column2: [Security features] Why disable unused switch ports?
column3: Stops someone plugging in an unauthorized device; also put them in an unused VLAN
Network Access Control — checks identity and device posture (patches, AV) before granting network access; can quarantine non-compliant devices
Limits which/how many MAC addresses can use a switch port; violations can shut the port (err-disable)
Protect (drop silently), Restrict (drop + log/count), Shutdown (err-disable the port — default)
Port security learns the connected device's MAC dynamically and saves it as allowed
Supplicant (client), authenticator (switch/AP), authentication server (RADIUS)
Port-based network access control — the port passes no normal traffic until the device authenticates via EAP to a RADIUS server

column2: [Security features] MAC filtering — why it's weak
column3: MAC addresses are easily spoofed; it's a deterrent, not real security
Securely generating, distributing, storing, rotating and revoking cryptographic keys/certificates
Ordered list of permit/deny rules on a router/firewall interface, matched top-down; the first match wins
Anything not explicitly permitted is denied at the end of the list
A broad permit placed above a specific deny makes the deny useless — put specific rules first
Blocks/allows websites by URL or category
Inspects content (keywords, file types, malware) and blocks inappropriate or dangerous material
Trusted: internal network. Untrusted: internet. Firewalls control traffic between zones
A separate zone for public-facing servers (web, mail) between the internet and the internal network, so a compromise there doesn't expose internal hosts
Identify the problem
Establish a theory of probable cause
Test the theory to determine the cause
Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem, and identify potential effects
Implement the solution or escalate as necessary
Gather information, question users, identify symptoms, determine if anything changed, duplicate the problem, approach multiple problems individually
Question the obvious; consider multiple approaches — top-to-bottom/bottom-to-top OSI, divide and conquer

column2: [Methodology] Step 3: the theory is confirmed — next?
column3: Determine the next steps to resolve the problem (move to the plan of action)

column2: [Methodology] Step 3: the theory is NOT confirmed — next?
column3: Establish a new theory or escalate

column2: [Methodology] What comes right after implementing the solution?
column3: Verify full system functionality and, if applicable, implement preventive measures
Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned

column2: [Methodology] When do you identify potential effects of a fix?
column3: Step 4 — while establishing the plan of action (before implementing)
Start troubleshooting in the middle of the OSI model (e.g. ping, layer 3) and move up or down depending on the result

column2: [Methodology] Scenario: a user reports the internet is down — the very first thing to do
column3: Gather information: question the user, identify symptoms, ask what changed (Step 1)

column2: [Cabling] Symptoms of using the wrong cable category for the speed
column3: Link negotiates lower speed, errors, or intermittent drops (e.g. Cat5 on a 1 Gbps or Cat5e on 10GBASE-T at length)

column2: [Cabling] Single-mode transceiver on multimode fiber (or vice versa)
column3: Mismatch → no link or high errors; transceiver type, fiber type and wavelength must match on both ends
Signal loss over distance — too long a run (copper > 100 m) causes errors/drops
Signal from one pair bleeding into another (NEXT/FEXT) — often from untwisting too much at termination
Electrical noise from motors, fluorescent lights, power cables — use shielded cable or fiber, reroute
Wrong pinout, untwisted pairs, bad crimp → no link, errors, or low speed. Re-terminate and test with a cable tester

column2: [Cabling] Fiber link has no light/connectivity after install — common simple cause
column3: TX and RX reversed — swap the strands (also check dirty connectors)
Corrupted frames — bad cable/connector, EMI, or duplex mismatch
Frames smaller than 64 bytes — usually collisions/duplex mismatch
Frames larger than the max (1518 bytes) — MTU/jumbo frame mismatch
Frames thrown away — usually congestion/buffers full (or errors)
Switch shut the port due to a violation (port security, BPDU guard, etc.) — fix the cause, then shut / no shut
Someone disabled it with 'shutdown' — enable with 'no shutdown'
Typically a link-aggregation member whose settings don't match the bundle (LACP misconfig)
The switch's total PoE capacity is used up — new PoE devices don't power on. Upgrade switch/PSU or rebalance
Device needs more power than the port supplies (e.g. PoE+ device on an 802.3af port) — won't power or keeps rebooting
Optical power too low (dirty/damaged connectors, too long, bad splices) or too high (short SMF run without attenuator)

column2: [Cabling] Cat 5/6/7/8 issue on the exam: 10 Gbps needed for a 90 m run — which category?
column3: Cat6a (Cat6 only does 10G to ~55 m; Cat8 only ~30 m)

column2: [Cabling] STP vs UTP issue: new run beside heavy machinery keeps erroring
column3: Use shielded twisted pair (grounded) or fiber

column2: [Service issues] Symptoms of a switching loop
column3: Broadcast storm, very high utilization/CPU, MAC address flapping, network-wide outage

column2: [Service issues] Suboptimal root bridge (e.g. an old access switch became root)
column3: Traffic takes inefficient paths — set the core switch's priority lowest so it's always root

column2: [Service issues] STP issue: port stuck blocking/forwarding when it shouldn't
column3: Check port roles/states and costs; a wrongly forwarding port causes a loop, a wrongly blocked one cuts connectivity

column2: [Service issues] Host is on the wrong VLAN — symptom
column3: Gets an address from the wrong subnet (or APIPA) and can't reach its normal resources

column2: [Service issues] Traffic to one service fails but everything else works
column3: Check ACLs/firewall rules for that port/protocol

column2: [Service issues] Can reach local hosts but nothing on other networks
column3: Incorrect or missing default gateway

column2: [Service issues] Router can't reach a remote network but has internet
column3: Missing route in the routing table (or the default route is the only path)

column2: [Service issues] Several new clients get 169.254.x.x addresses
column3: DHCP scope/address pool exhausted (or DHCP server unreachable)

column2: [Service issues] Intermittent connectivity and 'address conflict' warnings
column3: Duplicate IP address — two hosts with the same IP (often a static IP inside a DHCP scope)

column2: [Service issues] Host can reach some hosts on its own subnet but not others
column3: Incorrect subnet mask

column2: [Service issues] Host has the right IP and gateway but can't resolve names (ping by IP works)
column3: DNS problem — wrong/unreachable DNS server
Bandwidth: theoretical capacity of the link. Throughput: what you actually get
Delay for data to travel from source to destination (ms)
Variation in latency between packets — ruins voice/video
Packets that never arrive — causes retransmits (TCP) or gaps (voice/video)
More traffic than a link or device can handle → queuing, latency, drops
The slowest link/device in the path limits overall throughput
One-way latency < 150 ms, jitter < 30 ms, packet loss < 1%
Microwave ovens, Bluetooth, cordless phones, baby monitors, neighboring networks
Nearby APs on the same or overlapping channels compete (co-channel/adjacent-channel interference) — use 1/6/11, narrower widths, more 5 GHz
Distance and obstacles (walls, metal, water, glass) weaken signal → low data rates, drops
Dead spots — site survey, add/move APs, adjust power/antennas
Clients repeatedly dropping off — interference, weak signal, misconfig, or a deauthentication attack
APs with different SSIDs/security settings, or bad power levels causing 'sticky' clients that cling to a distant AP
Measured in negative dBm — closer to 0 is stronger. About −67 dBm or better for voice/video; −80 is poor; −90 unusable
Captures and decodes packets for analysis — Wireshark (GUI), tcpdump (CLI)
Tests reachability and round-trip time with ICMP echo request/reply
ping -t   (Windows sends 4 by default)

column2: [Tools] ping a set number of times on Linux
column3: ping -c 4   (Linux pings until Ctrl+C by default)
Shows each router hop to a destination by sending probes with increasing TTL and reading ICMP Time Exceeded replies
Linux traceroute: UDP by default. Windows tracert: ICMP echo
Queries DNS — test name resolution, specify a server, look up record types (set type=mx)
Linux/Unix DNS query tool with detailed output (dig example.com MX, dig @8.8.8.8 example.com)
CLI packet capture (tcpdump -i eth0 port 53 -w cap.pcap)
Shows active connections, listening ports, routing table and stats (netstat -an; -r routes; -b process on Windows)
/all full config; /release and /renew DHCP; /flushdns clear DNS cache; /displaydns show it
ip addr, ip route, ip link, ip neigh (ARP); ifconfig is the legacy equivalent
Shows/edits the IP → MAC cache: arp -a
Network scanner — host discovery, open ports, service versions, OS detection (nmap -sV -O host)
Neighbor discovery protocols — a device advertises its name, model, port, IP, VLAN to directly connected neighbors. LLDP = open standard, CDP = Cisco
Measures actual throughput/latency to a server (speedtest, iperf)
Puts a tone on a cable so you can find the other end in a bundle/patch panel
Checks continuity, pinout (miswires, opens, shorts) of copper cables; certifiers also test performance
Time-domain reflectometer — finds the distance to a break/fault in copper (TDR) or fiber (OTDR)
Hardware device inline on a link that copies all traffic to a monitoring tool
Shows SSIDs, channels, signal strength, interference — used for channel planning and troubleshooting
Shines visible red laser into fiber to find breaks/sharp bends and check continuity
